value: negative phototaxis at 400 nm rose with irradiance, reaching 57.14 ± 7.14% at 600 µW cm-2 (Y-tube, adults)
units: % of tested adults in the dark arm
method: Y-tube phototaxis screening with wavelength-specific LED lamps; positive phototaxis = L/N x 100 and negative phototaxis = D/N x 100, where N includes insects left in the base arm
conditions: 25 ± 2 °C and 70 ± 5% relative humidity (Methods; the Abstract gives 25 ± 1 °C); adults collected after mating and sexed, sex used in assays not reported, age and feeding status not stated; 30 min dark adaptation; irradiance varied between 100 and 1000 µW cm-2 in screening (per the page summary); the page does not say whether arm sides were swapped or randomised, and the lighting of the dark arm is not described; the ± term is not defined in the quoted sentence; in the same Results paragraph negative phototaxis was concentrated at 400 and 440 nm, and under several longer-wavelength conditions the difference between positive and negative phototaxis was reduced or reversed; laboratory Y-tube only, the Discussion calls for field or greenhouse validation

value: stage 48/49 tadpoles most often found with 3 or 4 of the 10 tadpoles in the green quadrant of a dish (green preference over white)
method: open-field group assay: 10 tadpoles in a 140 mm dish on an LCD monitor projecting one coloured quadrant (about 25% of the floor) with the other three quadrants white or black; occupancy recorded over the trial
conditions: wild-type tadpoles from in-house matings or a commercial supplier, stage 48/49, never fed, colour preference run on tadpoles 13 to 18 days post-fertilization; 30 min per trial; 2 of 78 trials excluded; each group of 10 tested once (ablated groups twice); whether quadrant positions or colour order were randomised or rotated is not stated in the Methods (page summary); from a paraphrased Results sentence, about 32.4% of tadpoles were in the green quadrant against about 24.4% in the matching quadrant of an all-white dish (p = 0.02, Mann-Whitney U with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment); the preference is modest, and preferences for red and against blue were not statistically significant (paraphrased); the paper reports that slower swimming in green accounts for the preference; the quote gives no percent or p-value

value: free-moving workers acquired a conditioned proboscis-extension response (PER) to guava odour more strongly than to mango odour
method: olfactory PER conditioning of free-moving workers in mini-cages (fmPER): guava or mango odour paired with 50% w/v sucrose reward, lavender used as a novel odour control, over two days; harnessed bees did not show conditioned PER
conditions: the number of bees, groups and colonies is not stated in the article (page summary); workers were collected at a hive entrance; learning of an odour-reward association, so this shows odour detection and discrimination through a conditioned response, not a detection threshold; the Discussion reports, in fragments, an average conditioned-PER probability of 75% for guava and 40% for mango by the sixth trial; on day 1 conditioned responses were low and the effect of the scented reward was not a significant factor on day 2 (Abstract); individual bee differences were significant and not explained by the fixed factors, and age and health were not controlled (authors, per page summary)

value: midbrain auditory evoked potentials most sensitive between about 20 and 28 kHz (ultrasonic)
method: auditory evoked potentials recorded from the torus semicircularis of six males with tone bursts from 2 to about 40 kHz in 1 kHz steps, in an anechoic sound isolation chamber
conditions: six males (n = 6); animals were surgically prepared with the head placed on crushed ice to limit bleeding; no threshold criterion and no threshold in dB SPL are reported (the paper reports a calibration level only), and the measure is peak-to-peak AEP amplitude, so the value is a sensitivity maximum and not a threshold audiogram; recording temperature not reported; the authors note that the playback part of the study did not characterise responses to audible calls, so discrimination of ultrasonic from audible conspecific calls is not shown (paraphrased); in the field playback (seven males with complete data sets) males called more to ultrasound-only broadcasts than to background, Wilcoxon Signed Ranks P = .043 (ending of a longer sentence, page summary)

value: fifth-instar larvae: sinigrin was the most effective glucosinolate feeding stimulant at 1e-4 M, preference index 0.89 ± 0.030
units: preference index (treated consumed area / total consumed area; 0.5 = no preference)
method: two-choice leaf-disc feeding assay: 20 uL glucosinolate in water on the treated disc against 20 uL water on the control disc, four 1.5 cm cowpea leaf discs from one leaf in a 9.0 cm Petri dish, one fifth-instar larva placed at the centre
conditions: the Methods do not state the number of larvae per replicate or any starvation period (page summary); the ± term is not defined in the quoted sentence; the stimulatory activity of sinigrin, gluconapin, glucoiberin and gluconasturtiin started at a lower dose than glucobrassicin, which started at 1e-4 M (ending of a longer Results sentence); electrophysiology in the same paper: larval lateral sensilla styloconica responded to sinigrin at 10 mM while medial sensilla did not, and adult lateral tarsal sensilla did not respond at 10 mM (paraphrased, spike values only in figures); these are not part of this record
